title: BFS on an Implicit Graph: Word Ladder
oneLiner: The fewest one-letter changes from one word to another: the words are nodes, "differs by one letter" is an edge, and BFS finds the shortest path.
keyTakeaway: Nobody hands you the graph, but it is there: each word is a node, and two words are joined when they differ in exactly one position. Every step costs the same, so BFS finds the shortest ladder. To find a word's neighbours fast, group the word list by wildcard patterns ("hot" belongs to "*ot", "h*t" and "ho*"): words in the same bucket are exactly one change apart.
explanation:
Given beginWord, endWord and a list of allowed words, a ladder changes one letter at a time, and every word after beginWord (including endWord) must be in wordList. Return the number of words in the shortest ladder, counting both ends, or 0 if there is none. All words have the same length and use lowercase letters. beginWord does not have to be in the list. For "hit" to "cog" with [hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog] the answer is 5: hit, hot, dot, dog, cog.

Treat it as a graph. The nodes are the words, and there is an edge between two words that differ in exactly one position. Each change costs one step, so "shortest ladder" is "shortest path in an unweighted graph", which is what BFS gives you: it explores every word 1 change away, then every word 2 changes away, and so on, so the first time it dequeues endWord it has found the shortest ladder. DFS would find some ladder, not necessarily the shortest.

The part that needs thought is finding neighbours without building every edge. Comparing a word with every other word costs O(n · L) per word and O(n² · L) overall. Instead, build wildcard buckets once: for each word and each position i, replace letter i with '*' and add the word to that pattern's bucket. "hot" goes into "*ot", "h*t" and "ho*"; "dot" goes into "*ot", "d*t" and "do*". Two words are neighbours exactly when they share a bucket, so during BFS you generate the current word's L patterns and read the words in those buckets. Building each pattern costs O(L), so the total is O(n · L²) time and O(n · L²) space for the buckets. (The other common approach tries all 26 letters at every position and checks a set: O(n · 26 · L²), which is fine for lowercase words.)

The BFS itself: if endWord isn't in the list, return 0 straight away. Start the queue with (beginWord, 1) and mark it visited. Dequeue (word, length); if word is endWord, return length. Otherwise, for each pattern of word, enqueue every unvisited word in that bucket with length + 1, marking it visited as it is enqueued. A useful extra: once a bucket has been read, empty it. Every word in it is now visited, so reading it again later would only find words to skip. If the queue runs out, return 0.

Faster still is bidirectional BFS: search from both ends at once, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stop when the two meet. A related follow-up returns every shortest ladder, not just the length, which needs the BFS to record each word's parents. The visualization runs the example above; the label under each node is its word and its ladder length once BFS reaches it.

visualizationSteps.message: Words one letter apart are joined. The graph isn't given: BFS discovers it through buckets like "*ot" = [hot, dot, lot], "do*" = [dot, dog] and "*og" = [dog, log, cog], built once from the word list.
Start the queue with hit at ladder length 1 and mark it visited.
Dequeue hit (length 1). Its non-empty buckets: "h*t". Enqueue the unvisited word hot at length 2, then empty that bucket.
Dequeue hot (length 2). Its non-empty buckets: "*ot", "ho*". Enqueue the unvisited words dot and lot at length 3, then empty those buckets.
Dequeue dot (length 3). Its non-empty buckets: "d*t", "do*". Enqueue the unvisited word dog at length 4, then empty those buckets.
Dequeue lot (length 3). Its non-empty buckets: "l*t", "lo*". Enqueue the unvisited word log at length 4, then empty those buckets.
Dequeue dog (length 4). Its non-empty buckets: "*og", "d*g". Enqueue the unvisited word cog at length 5, then empty those buckets.
Dequeue log (length 4). Its non-empty buckets: "l*g". Every word in it is already visited, so nothing new is enqueued.
Dequeue cog at length 5: that is the answer. Following parents back gives hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog. BFS reached it in the first layer it could, so no shorter ladder exists.

recognitionSignals: "Fewest steps", "minimum number of moves" or "shortest sequence" where every move costs the same, but the states are words, combinations, or board positions instead of graph nodes.
You can describe one move (change one letter, turn one dial, swap two tiles) but you are not given an edge list: the graph is implicit and you generate neighbours on the fly.
A list of allowed or forbidden states that every intermediate step must respect.
gotchas: Mark a word visited when you ENQUEUE it, not when you dequeue it. Otherwise the same word can sit in the queue many times and the search slows down badly.
The answer counts words, not changes: hit -> hot is a ladder of 2. Start the length at 1 for beginWord.
If endWord is not in wordList there is no valid ladder at all, even when it is one letter away from beginWord. Return 0.
Comparing every pair of words to build edges is O(n² · L) and times out on large lists; generate neighbours through wildcard buckets (or by trying 26 letters per position) instead.
confusableWith: Grid BFS: Rotting Oranges (this track) is also BFS counting layers, but on a grid where the neighbours are given by geometry. Here working out who the neighbours are is half the problem.
Dijkstra's Algorithm finds shortest paths when steps cost different amounts. Every change here costs 1, so plain BFS is enough and simpler.
Backtracking: Word Search (this track) also builds words letter by letter, but it has to explore every path and undo choices. A shortest-path question wants BFS, which never revisits a word.

complexity.note: n words of length L each make L patterns, and building or hashing a pattern costs O(L), so filling and reading the buckets is O(n · L²). The buckets hold n · L word references keyed by patterns of length L.
